name: Kannada

script.overview:
Kannada script (ಕನ್ನಡ ಲಿಪಿ) is an **abugida**, a close cousin of the Telugu script. Each consonant letter carries an inherent vowel **a**: ಕ is *ka*. To get other vowels you attach a **vowel sign** (ಕಾಗುಣಿತ *kāguṇita*): ಕ *ka*, ಕಾ *kā*, ಕಿ *ki*, ಕೀ *kī*, ಕು *ku*, ಕೂ *kū*, ಕೆ *ke*, ಕೇ *kē* and so on. Independent vowel letters (ಅ ಆ ಇ ...) are used only at the start of a word.

Most letters have a little horizontal tick on top called the **ತಲೆಕಟ್ಟು** *talekaṭṭu* ('head-tie'); it represents the inherent *a*. When you add the i-sign, the tick is replaced by a curl (ಕ → ಕಿ). The script is written left to right, with no capital letters, and the letters are very round, because they were historically scratched on palm leaves, where straight lines would split the leaf.

To write a consonant **without** a vowel you add the **halant** ್ (ಕ್). When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, the second is usually written as a small **ottakshara** (ಒತ್ತಕ್ಷರ, 'pressed letter') **below** the first: ಕ + ್ + ಕ = ಕ್ಕ (*kka*), ಅಮ್ಮ *amma*, ಪುಸ್ತಕ *pustaka*. A ರ before another consonant is written as a small hook after the cluster (ಅರ್ಕಾವೊತ್ತು), as in ಧರ್ಮ *dharma*. Mastering the ottaksharas is the main hurdle in reading Kannada, but there are only about 35 subscript shapes and most look like shrunken versions of the full letter.

The traditional alphabet (ಅಕ್ಷರಮಾಲೆ *akṣaramāle*) has 49 letters: 13 vowels (ಸ್ವರ), 2 'carriers' ಂ and ಃ (ಯೋಗವಾಹ), and 34 consonants (ವ್ಯಂಜನ), divided into 25 *vargīya* (grouped, arranged by mouth position) and 9 *avargīya* (ungrouped). Kannada also has its own digits ೦–೯, though Western digits are now more common in everyday use.

groups.title: Kannada digits (ಅಂಕಿಗಳು)
groups.note: Native digits appear on government documents, older signs, calendars and school books. Western digits are more common day to day.

speakers: ≈44 million L1; ≈60 million including L2 speakers
where: Karnataka (south-western India) and neighbouring border districts of Maharashtra, Goa, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; large diaspora in the Gulf, USA and UK
tagline: The language of Bengaluru, Mysuru and over a thousand years of literature, with one of the most logical, beautiful scripts in India.
intro:
**Kannada** (ಕನ್ನಡ) is a **Dravidian** language, a sister of Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam. It is the official language of Karnataka and the everyday language of Bengaluru, Mysuru, Hubballi-Dharwad and Mangaluru. Its literature goes back over a thousand years, and it has won more Jnanpith awards than any Indian language except Hindi.

Kannada is **agglutinative**: meaning is built by stacking suffixes onto a root (ಮನೆ *mane* 'house' → ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ *maneyalli* 'in the house' → ಮನೆಗಳಲ್ಲಿ *manegaḷalli* 'in the houses'). The basic word order is **subject–object–verb**, verbs agree with the subject in person, number and gender, and there is no ergative construction. Like all Dravidian languages it borrowed heavily from Sanskrit, so many 'learned' words will look familiar to Hindi speakers.

Kannada has a noticeable gap between **written standard** and **everyday speech**. Books and news say ಹೋಗುತ್ತೇನೆ *hōguttēne* 'I will go'; people in Bengaluru say ಹೋಗ್ತೀನಿ *hōgtīni*. In North Karnataka and in rural speech you will also hear forms like ಐತೆ *aite* for standard ಇದೆ *ide* 'there is'. This course gives the **neutral standard** form in vocabulary lists and grammar tables, and the **natural spoken Bengaluru/Mysuru form** in phrases and dialogues, with the other form in the notes, so you can both read a newspaper and chat at a darshini.

Kannada has two registers of 'you': **ನೀನು** *nīnu* (informal: friends, children, close family) and **ನೀವು** *nīvu* (polite, and plural). Start with ನೀವು with everyone you don't know well.
romanizationNote: Romanization follows pronunciation. A macron marks a long vowel: Kannada contrasts short and long versions of **a, i, u, e and o**, including **e/ē** and **o/ō** (ಬೆಳೆ *beḷe* 'crop' vs ಬೇಳೆ *bēḷe* 'lentils'), so never ignore it. A dot under a consonant means retroflex (tongue curled back): ṭ ḍ ṇ ḷ; plain t d n l are dental (tongue touching the teeth). ಶ is written *sh* and ಷ is *ṣ*, but in modern speech both sound like English 'sh'. *ch* is always as in 'church'. Doubled letters (*tt, kk, ll*) are genuinely held longer. *h* after a consonant (*kh, th, dh, bh*) means aspiration, mostly in Sanskrit loans and often weakened in speech; in English loans written with ಫ (*ph*), most speakers say *f*: ಫೋನ್ *phōn* sounds like 'fōn', ಕಾಫಿ *kāphi* like 'kāfi'. ಋ is written *ru* because that is how it is pronounced. Word-initial *e* and *o* are often pronounced with a little glide (ಎಲ್ಲಿ *elli* sounds like 'yelli', ಒಂದು *ondu* like 'wondu'), but the romanization does not show it.

pronunciation.title: Short and long vowels: a/ā, i/ī, u/ū
pronunciation.body:
In Kannada, vowel length changes meaning. A long vowel is held roughly twice as long as a short one, and the quality stays essentially the same (unlike English, where 'long' and 'short' vowels are different sounds).

The one exception is *a*: short *a* is a neutral 'uh' (as in 'cup'); long *ā* is the open 'aa' of 'father'. Short *i* and *u* are tense but brief; *ī* and *ū* are held.

English speakers tend to shorten unstressed long vowels. In Kannada, a long vowel stays long wherever it is in the word: ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು *beṅgaḷūru* has a long *ū* in the third syllable.
tips: Clap twice for a long vowel, once for a short one.
Short a is 'uh', not 'aa': ಮರ mara is 'muh-ruh'.
Keep the vowel quality the same; just hold it longer.

pronunciation.title: Short and long e and o
pronunciation.body:
Unlike Hindi, Kannada has both **short e/o** and **long ē/ō**, and they distinguish words. The script marks them clearly (ೆ vs ೇ, ೊ vs ೋ), and this course marks long ones with a macron.

Short *e* is like the e in 'bed' but tenser; long *ē* is like 'ay' in 'say' without sliding into a y. Short *o* is like 'o' in 'obey'; long *ō* is a pure 'oh' without the w-glide of English 'go'.

Grammar depends on it too: ಇದೆ *ide* 'it is (there)' vs ಇದೇ *idē* 'this very one'; the ending of ಮಾಡಿದೆ *māḍide* 'I did' has a short e, while ಮಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ *māḍuttēne* 'I will do' has a long ē.
tips: Never diphthongize: the ē of ಏಳು ēḷu does not slide into a y at the end like English 'ay'.
Final -e in Kannada is always short and clear: ಮನೆ mane = 'muh-neh'.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental: ṭ ḍ ṇ vs t d n
pronunciation.body:
Kannada has two complete sets of 't, d, n' sounds. **Dental** ತ ದ ನ: the tongue tip presses against the back of the upper teeth (as in French or Spanish). **Retroflex** ಟ ಡ ಣ: the tongue tip curls back and touches the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge, giving a hollow, 'dark' sound.

English t and d sit between the two, so to a Kannada ear they sound vaguely retroflex. Indian English 't' is actually Kannada ಟ. To get it right, exaggerate: really put your tongue on your teeth for ತ, and really curl it back for ಟ.

Retroflex sounds also colour the vowel before them, and between vowels ಡ often becomes a soft flap.
tips: For ತ/ದ, you should feel your tongue touch your teeth.
For ಟ/ಡ/ಣ, curl the tongue tip up and back as if saying 'r' then release.
Indian English 'T' in 'TV' is ಟ; the 'th' in 'thin' minus the hiss is close to ತ.

pronunciation.title: ಳ vs ಲ: the retroflex l
pronunciation.body:
ಲ *l* is a clear l with the tongue tip on the gum ridge or teeth. ಳ *ḷ* is made by curling the tongue tip back (as for ಟ) and letting air flow round the sides. It sounds darker and heavier, a bit like an l pronounced while thinking of an r.

ಳ never begins a word but is very common in the middle and at the end: ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು, ಮಳೆ 'rain', ಹೇಳು 'tell', ಕೇಳು 'ask'. Some urban speakers merge ಳ into ಲ, but this is considered careless and creates real confusion, as the pairs show.
tips: Say 'ṭa' and slide into an l without moving the tongue tip forward.
Listen for ಳ in the name of the city: Bengaḷūru.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration (kh, gh, th, dh, ph, bh)
pronunciation.body:
Kannada script has a full set of aspirated letters (ಖ ಘ ಛ ಝ ಠ ಢ ಥ ಧ ಫ ಭ), but native Dravidian words never use them. They appear in **Sanskrit, Hindi, Persian and English loans**: ಭಾಷೆ *bhāṣe*, ಧನ್ಯವಾದ *dhanyavāda*, ಖುಷಿ *khuṣi*.

In careful speech (news, teachers, educated Mysuru speech) aspiration is pronounced. In everyday speech it is often **weakened or lost**: ಕಥೆ 'story' is very often written ಕತೆ, and ಭಾಷೆ often sounds like 'bāṣe'. As a learner, aim for light aspiration on these words: it sounds educated, but nobody will misunderstand you without it.

The flip side: **unaspirated** ಕ ಟ ತ ಪ must have *no* puff of air. English speakers aspirate initial p/t/k ('pin', 'tin'); in Kannada that can sound like a different letter. Hold your hand in front of your mouth: for ಪ ಕ ತ you should feel almost no air.
tips: Say ಪ like the p in 'spin', not 'pin'.
For ಭ ಧ ಘ, add a breathy h *during* the release, not after.
Don't worry if natives drop aspiration; it's normal.

pairs.note: The same word: shows how aspiration is lost in everyday Kannada.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants (gemination)
pronunciation.body:
Doubled consonants are everywhere in Kannada: ಅಮ್ಮ, ಅಪ್ಪ, ಅಕ್ಕ, ಅಣ್ಣ, ಇಲ್ಲ, ಎಲ್ಲಿ. A double consonant is **held** for about twice as long, the way English joins the two t's in 'cat-tail'. The vowel before a double consonant is short and crisp.

Getting this wrong changes words: ಕತೆ *kate* is 'story' but ಕತ್ತೆ *katte* is 'donkey'. Don't be the person telling a donkey.
tips: Pause briefly on the consonant: ak-ka, am-ma, il-la.
For doubled stops, hold the closure silently before releasing.

pronunciation.title: Final -u, -e, -a: every word ends in a vowel
pronunciation.body:
Native Kannada words almost always end in a vowel, and that vowel is pronounced clearly. Unlike Hindi, the final *a* is **not** dropped: ಮರ is *mara* (tree), not 'mar'. Final -e is a clean short e: ಮನೆ *mane*, never 'main'.

Many words end in a short **-u**, which in fast speech is light and slightly unrounded (almost like a short 'ɨ'), but don't drop it: ಕರು *karu* 'calf' and ಕರೆ *kare* 'call' are different words. Kannada even adds an -u to English loans ending in a consonant: ಬಸ್ಸು *bassu* 'bus', ಕಾರು *kāru* 'car', ಫ್ಯಾನು *phyānu* 'fan'.

Final vowels matter grammatically: ಮಾಡು *māḍu* 'do!' (informal) vs ಮಾಡಿ *māḍi* 'please do' (polite).
tips: Pronounce every final vowel, briefly.
The final -u is short and relaxed, not a full 'oo'.

pronunciation.title: Initial e and o: the y- and w-glides
pronunciation.body:
In natural speech, a word beginning with ಎ/ಏ is usually pronounced with a light *y* in front, and a word beginning with ಒ/ಓ with a light *w*: ಎಲ್ಲಿ 'yelli', ಏನು 'yēnu', ಒಂದು 'wondu', ಓದು 'wōdu'. This is how Kannadigas sound, and copying it will make you sound natural. Spelling is unaffected.

The same glides smooth over vowel meetings inside words and between suffixes: ಮನೆ + ಅಲ್ಲಿ → ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ *maneyalli* 'in the house' (a written ಯ appears), ಗುರು + ಅನ್ನು → ಗುರುವನ್ನು *guruvannu* (a written ವ appears).
tips: Don't overdo it: the glide is light.
Learn the written ಯ/ವ glides in case endings: ಮನೆಯ, ಗುರುವಿನ.

pairs.note: y-glide inserted before a vowel suffix

pronunciation.title: ಸ, ಶ, ಷ and Sanskrit clusters
pronunciation.body:
ಸ is a plain *s*. ಶ and ಷ were once different (palatal vs retroflex), but in modern Kannada both are simply **sh**. Spelling still distinguishes them, so learn each word's spelling, but pronounce both as 'sh'. Some speakers, especially in rural areas, merge ಶ into ಸ ('sāle' for ಶಾಲೆ), which is considered non-standard.

The Sanskrit clusters ಕ್ಷ and ಜ್ಞ have special pronunciations: ಕ್ಷ = 'ksh' (ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆ *parīkṣe* 'exam'), and ಜ್ಞ is usually 'gny' or 'jn' (ಜ್ಞಾನ 'gnyāna'). ಋ is said 'ru' (ಕೃಷ್ಣ *kruṣṇa*).
tips: ಶ = ಷ = 'sh' in practice.
Keep ಸ (s) and ಶ (sh) apart: they make different words.

pronunciation.title: The anusvara ಂ and nasal assimilation
pronunciation.body:
The little circle ಂ (anusvara, called ಸೊನ್ನೆ 'zero') is a nasal consonant whose exact sound depends on the next letter: it becomes **ṅ** (ng) before ಕ/ಗ, **ñ** before ಚ/ಜ, **ṇ** before ಟ/ಡ, **n** before ತ/ದ, and **m** before ಪ/ಬ and at the end of a word or before ವ/ಸ/ಹ etc.

Kannada does **not** use it for nasalized vowels as Hindi does; it is always a real consonant. So ಅಂಗಡಿ is *aṅgaḍi* (with a real 'ng' + g), and ಚಂದ is *chanda*.
tips: Read ಂ as the nasal that matches the next consonant.
Before s, h, v, y, r, l it usually sounds like 'm'.

pronunciation.title: Written vs spoken Kannada
pronunciation.body:
Kannada speech contracts the long written verb forms. The most important patterns (Bengaluru/Mysuru standard): the present/future suffix -ಉತ್ತ- shrinks to -ತ್-, and the endings -ಏನೆ / -ಏವೆ become -ಈನಿ / -ಈವಿ. So ಮಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ *māḍuttēne* → ಮಾಡ್ತೀನಿ *māḍtīni* 'I do / will do'; ಬರುತ್ತಾರೆ *baruttāre* → ಬರ್ತಾರೆ *bartāre* 'they come'. ಅದು 'it' takes -ಉತ್ತೆ: ಆಗುತ್ತದೆ → ಆಗುತ್ತೆ *āgutte*.

Case endings and negatives shrink too: ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ → ಮನೇಲಿ *manēli*, ಮನೆಯನ್ನು → ಮನೇನ *manēna*, ಮಾಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ → ಮಾಡಲ್ಲ *māḍalla*.

Regional speech differs again: in North Karnataka and rural Mysuru areas you'll hear ಐತೆ *aite* for ಇದೆ *ide* 'is/there is', ಹೋಗ್ತೀನಿ vs ಹೋಗ್ತೇನಿ, etc. This course teaches the Bengaluru/Mysuru spoken forms for conversation; they are understood everywhere.
tips: Read in written forms; speak in contracted forms.
The rhythm of spoken Kannada is quick: listen for -ತೀನಿ, -ತಾರೆ, -ತೀರ.

pronunciation.title: Stress, rhythm and question intonation
pronunciation.body:
Kannada has a light, even rhythm. Stress usually falls on the **first syllable**, and every syllable keeps its full vowel: there's no swallowing of unstressed vowels as in English. Long vowels and double consonants make syllables 'heavy', and that heaviness is what gives Kannada its rhythm.

Yes/no questions are made by adding **-ಆ** *-ā* to the end of a sentence, with a **rising** pitch on it: ಬರ್ತೀರಾ? *bartīrā?* 'Will you come?'. Questions with a question word (ಏನು, ಎಲ್ಲಿ) have a falling intonation. The tag ಅಲ್ವಾ? *alvā?* 'isn't it?' rises.

Kannadigas frequently soften or end sentences with ಅಂತೆ *ante* 'apparently, they say', ಅಲ್ವಾ 'right?', and the friendly vocative ending -ಓ (to a man) / -ಏ (to a woman), e.g. ಬಾರೋ *bārō* 'come here, man!' (informal).
tips: Stress the first syllable lightly; don't reduce later vowels.
Make the -ā of yes/no questions rise clearly.

pronunciation.title: h-dropping and the history of ಹ
pronunciation.body:
Many native Kannada words begin with ಹ *h*: ಹಾಲು 'milk', ಹಣ್ಣು 'fruit', ಹೋಗು 'go', ಹೇಳು 'tell'. Historically, most of these had a *p* in Old Kannada (ಪಾಲ್ *pāl* 'milk', compare Tamil *pāl*), which softened to *h* roughly 900–1,000 years ago.

In some colloquial speech, especially rural speech of the Old Mysore region (Mandya, Mysuru, Ramanagara, Chamarajanagar and rural Bengaluru) and in casual fast talk, this *h* is weakened or dropped altogether: ಹಾಲು → 'ālu', ಹೋಗು → 'ōgu', ಹೇಳು → 'ēḷu'. Standard and educated Bengaluru speech keeps the h, and you should too, because dropping it can create a different word.
tips: Always pronounce initial ಹ in your own speech.
When listening, be ready for 'ōgi' = ಹೋಗಿ, 'ēḷi' = ಹೇಳಿ.
